"'''Wherever You Will Go'''" is a song by American band [[The Calling (band)|the Calling]]. It was released on May 22, 2001, as the first single from their debut studio album, ''[[Camino Palmero]]'' (2001). It remains their most successful hit, peaking at number five on the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and topping the [[Adult Top 40]] for 23 weeks, tied for the [[Adult Top 40#Most weeks at number one|third-longest]]-running number one in the chart's history, along with [[Taylor Swift]]'s "[[Cruel Summer (Taylor Swift song)|Cruel Summer]]" (2023).{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} Outside the United States, the song topped the music charts of Italy, New Zealand, and Poland, reached number three in the United Kingdom, peaked at number five in Australia, and became a top-10 hit in several European countries.

"Wherever You Will Go" is a song by American band the Calling. It was released on May 22, 2001, as the first single from their debut studio album, Camino Palmero (2001). It remains their most successful hit, peaking at number five on the US Billboard Hot 100 and topping the Adult Top 40 for 23 weeks, tied for the third-longest-running number one in the chart's history, along with Taylor Swift's "Cruel Summer" (2023).{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} Outside the United States, the song topped the music charts of Italy, New Zealand, and Poland, reached number three in the United Kingdom, peaked at number five in Australia, and became a top-10 hit in several European countries.

sections.heading: Background and writing
sections.wikitext:
Songwriter Aaron Kamin talked about "Wherever You Will Go" in a radio interview. He said: "At the time my grandmother's best friend had passed away and she left behind a husband of 50 or more years and I was at the funeral and afterwards I just started thinking of what it would be like to be him and have your whole life change so dramatically and not for the best in a matter of moments. Somebody that you live and grow with and are one with, just to be gone, is crazy and I figured all he ever thinks about probably is finding a way to get back to her or be with her or make sure she's alright or something like that. That was the sentiment behind that."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.songfacts.com/facts/the-calling/wherever-you-will-go|title=Wherever You Will Go by The Calling|website=Songfacts|access-date=December 8, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/4-times-a-cringey-2000s-hit-was-actually-a-perfect-pop-song/|title=4 Times a Cringey 2000s Hit Was Actually a Perfect Pop Song|first=Lauren|last=Boisvert|date=July 20, 2026|work=VICE}}</ref>

According to Kamin, "Wherever You Will Go" was overlooked until it was heard by Kathy Nelson, who was president of film music for the [[Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures|Walt Disney Motion Picture Group]] at the time. "Kathy apparently said, 'That song is a fucking monster. I need it in this movie I'm working on,'" Kamin told ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]''. The film in question was ''[[Coyote Ugly]]'' (2000). Lead singer [[Alex Band]] also said that after the track's inclusion in ''Coyote Ugly'', [[Ron Fair]], manager of A&R at RCA Records, invited the Calling to make an album.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/the-calling-wherever-you-will-go-interview-where-are-they-now-9577487/|title=Wherever Did They Go? Why The Calling Disappeared After Delivering One of 2001’s Biggest Hits|first=Taylor|last=Weatherby|date=May 25, 2021|work=Billboard|access-date=July 21, 2026}}</ref>

Songwriter Aaron Kamin talked about "Wherever You Will Go" in a radio interview. He said: "At the time my grandmother's best friend had passed away and she left behind a husband of 50 or more years and I was at the funeral and afterwards I just started thinking of what it would be like to be him and have your whole life change so dramatically and not for the best in a matter of moments. Somebody that you live and grow with and are one with, just to be gone, is crazy and I figured all he ever thinks about probably is finding a way to get back to her or be with her or make sure she's alright or something like that. That was the sentiment behind that."

According to Kamin, "Wherever You Will Go" was overlooked until it was heard by Kathy Nelson, who was president of film music for the Walt Disney Motion Picture Group at the time. "Kathy apparently said, 'That song is a fucking monster. I need it in this movie I'm working on,'" Kamin told Billboard. The film in question was Coyote Ugly (2000). Lead singer Alex Band also said that after the track's inclusion in Coyote Ugly, Ron Fair, manager of A&R at RCA Records, invited the Calling to make an album.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: Two videos were shot for this song. The first was set in Mexico. The other version, which is more popular, was directed by [[Gregory Dark]], and has the band performing in the concrete channel of the [[Los Angeles River]], while a teenage [[soap opera]] plays in the foreground. A teenage girl gets her boyfriend's name tattooed on her shoulder, but when she finds him cheating with another girl, she flies into a rage, destroying most of his belongings. At the end of the video, she is seen with a new boyfriend (male model and then-fledgling actor [[Drew Fuller]]) with a flower tattoo covering the name, as her jealous ex watches her from his car. The group's lead singer, [[Alex Band]], can also be seen in some scenes singing in the foreground of some of the storyline, such as when the girl is seen destroying the belongings.

The song was covered by English singer-songwriter [[Charlene Soraia]] for use in a [[Twinings]] advert in the United Kingdom. It was released in the UK as a [[Music download|digital download]] on September 30, 2011. On October 9, 2011, the song entered the [[UK Singles Chart]] at number 20 and peaked at number three two weeks later. It served as the lead single from Soraia's debut studio album, ''[[Moonchild (Charlene Soraia album)|Moonchild]]'' (2011).

sections.heading: In popular culture
sections.wikitext:
The song was featured in the 2000 film ''[[Coyote Ugly]]'' in the scene where Violet first sees Kevin. The Calling performs the song live.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thecallingband.com/blog/|title=Blog|author=Calling Band|website=thecallingband.com|access-date=March 26, 2015}}</ref>

In 2001, the [[CBS]] network used the song and video to promote the debut of ''[[The Guardian (TV series)|The Guardian]]''.

The song was used in a commercial promoting the [[National Hockey League]]'s [[2001 Stanley Cup playoffs]].<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tImWJpWCAcw |title=NHL Cup Crazy commercial 2001 |date=July 10, 2023 |last=Steven Walsh |access-date=January 22, 2025 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

The song was featured in the 2003 British comedy-drama film ''[[Love Actually]]'' during a scene in which Colin ([[Kris Marshall]]) participates in an orgy with a group of [[Wisconsin]]ite girls shortly after arriving in the United States.

The song plays during the final scenes of the series finale of ''[[Saving Grace (American TV series)|Saving Grace]]''.

The song plays in ''[[Smallville]]'' during the final scene of the episode "Metamorphosis" (Season 1 episode 2).

The song was parodied in ''[[Mad TV]]'' by several of the cast playing the Calling, [[Scott Stapp]] of [[Creed (band)|Creed]], [[Eddie Vedder]] of [[Pearl Jam]], and [[Ray Charles]], making fun of how all the singers' voices sound the same and they accuse each other of getting famous by imitating them.

This song is also featured in the popular South Korean drama ''[[I'm Sorry, I Love You]]'', starring [[So Ji-sub]] and [[Im Soo-jung]], and its soundtrack as well.

A cover of this song is also featured in the movie ''[[Unravel: A Swiss Side Love Story]]''.

In [[JK Rowling]]'s [[Cormoran Strike]] series, the song is used for Robin Ellacott's first dance with Matthew Cunliffe at their wedding in [[Lethal White]]. In [[Strike (TV series)|the TV adaptation]], the song is also played at their wedding reception.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.tunefind.com/show/strike/season-4/100628|title = Music from Strike (Aka C.B. Strike) S4E01}}</ref>
sections.text:
The song was featured in the 2000 film Coyote Ugly in the scene where Violet first sees Kevin. The Calling performs the song live.

In 2001, the CBS network used the song and video to promote the debut of The Guardian.

The song was used in a commercial promoting the National Hockey League's 2001 Stanley Cup playoffs.

The song was featured in the 2003 British comedy-drama film Love Actually during a scene in which Colin (Kris Marshall) participates in an orgy with a group of Wisconsinite girls shortly after arriving in the United States.

The song plays during the final scenes of the series finale of Saving Grace.

The song plays in Smallville during the final scene of the episode "Metamorphosis" (Season 1 episode 2).

The song was parodied in Mad TV by several of the cast playing the Calling, Scott Stapp of Creed, Eddie Vedder of Pearl Jam, and Ray Charles, making fun of how all the singers' voices sound the same and they accuse each other of getting famous by imitating them.

This song is also featured in the popular South Korean drama I'm Sorry, I Love You, starring So Ji-sub and Im Soo-jung, and its soundtrack as well.

A cover of this song is also featured in the movie Unravel: A Swiss Side Love Story.

In JK Rowling's Cormoran Strike series, the song is used for Robin Ellacott's first dance with Matthew Cunliffe at their wedding in Lethal White. In the TV adaptation, the song is also played at their wedding reception.
